claims.statement: HubSpot's legacy private apps documentation describes an access token, unique to each private app, that is sent as a Bearer token in the Authorization header and that does not change when scopes change.

sources.supports: Private apps allow you to use HubSpot's APIs to access specific data from your HubSpot account. You can authorize what each private app can request or change in your account, which will generate an access token that's unique to your app.
When making a call to one of the HubSpot API endpoints, set the value of the Authorization field to Bearer [YOUR_TOKEN].
sources.locator: Make API calls with your app's access token

sources.supports: Private app access tokens will be updated to reflect available scopes ... but the token string itself will not change.
sources.locator: Make API calls with your app's access token

claims.statement: A single scanner rule artifact (the TruffleHog hubspot_apikey v2 detector) treats a pat-na1- or pat-eu1- prefix followed by five hyphen-separated groups of 8-4-4-4-12 alphanumeric characters as a HubSpot private app token; no second independent artifact and no HubSpot page was found, so this is an unconfirmed lead and not a format claim.

sources.supports: keyPat: pat-(eu|na)1- followed by 8-4-4-4-12 alphanumeric groups; keywords pat-na1- and pat-eu1-.

claims.statement: HubSpot's legacy private apps page describes rotating the access token: a rotation creates a new token and the original expires, either immediately or about 7 days later, and HubSpot recommends rotating every six months.

sources.supports: If your access token is lost or otherwise compromised, you can rotate the token. A new access token will be created and the original access token will expire.
which will trigger an expiration of the token in 7 days.

claims.statement: HubSpot documents a POST request to /oauth/v2/private-apps/get/access-token-info that takes the private app access token in a tokenKey body field and returns the creating user, the Hub ID, the private app ID and the token's scopes.

sources.supports: make a POST request to /oauth/v2/private-apps/get/access-token-info. In the request body, include your access token:
sources.locator: View private app access token information

sources.supports: The response will include information about the user who created the token, the Hub ID of the account, the private app ID, and the scopes associated with the token.
sources.locator: View private app access token information

claims.statement: HubSpot states that private app access tokens are implemented on top of OAuth and can be passed to its client libraries as an access token; the page does not state that the token string has the same format as an OAuth access token.

sources.supports: Private app access tokens are implemented on top of OAuth, so you can also make authenticated calls with your access token using one of HubSpot's client libraries.
sources.locator: Make API calls with your app's access token

claims.statement: HubSpot's changelog, announced 2026-08-27, states that creation of new legacy private apps through the account UI is being permanently removed (2026-09-28 for accounts created on or after that date, 2026-10-26 for earlier accounts), that existing legacy private apps continue to work, and that Service Keys are the replacement for new in-account integrations.

sources.supports: HubSpot is permanently removing the ability to create new legacy, non-Project based, private apps through the account UI.
All existing legacy private apps continue to work as-is.

claims.statement: Two open-source scanner rule artifacts by different maintainers (Gitleaks and the TruffleHog version 1 HubSpot detector) both treat a value of five hyphen-separated groups of 8-4-4-4-12 characters, found near a HubSpot-related keyword, as a HubSpot API key or token (Gitleaks admits hexadecimal digits with a case-insensitive flag; TruffleHog admits letters and digits). Neither artifact says which HubSpot credential it targets, and this records consistency of those artifacts only, not a private app token format.

openQuestions.question: This candidate is not researched beyond existence: the pages read name the credential but state no literal prefix, alphabet, length or checksum, and no format is recorded or inferred.
Whether the legacy private app access token and the static auth access token are one credential family or two is not settled by the pages read; they are kept as two candidates.

Whether private app (and static auth) access tokens carry a pat-na1- or pat-eu1- prefix is unconfirmed: HubSpot pages read show masked or placeholder values only, and only one scanner maintainer's artifact (the TruffleHog v2 detector) shows the prefix. It needs a second independent artifact or a HubSpot statement.

No HubSpot page read states a prefix, alphabet, length, grouping or region marker for a private app access token. Whether private app tokens issued in different eras or regions begin pat-na1- or pat-eu1-, or are UUID-shaped, is unresolved; the pat- lead rests on one maintainer's detector (version 2) and the UUID-shaped lead names no specific HubSpot credential. A HubSpot statement, or two independent maintainers' artifacts that target private app tokens, would settle it.

A search of the Kingfisher, Nosey Parker and Gitleaks rule sets at the commits read found no rule for the pat-na1- or pat-eu1- form; the Kingfisher HubSpot rule is imported from the Gitleaks UUID-shaped rule and counts once with it.

The legacy private apps page describes a token shown on a private app's Auth tab under Legacy apps; the authentication overview describes a static auth access token found in app settings, configured with auth type static and private distribution. Neither page mentions the other credential and neither states that the two strings share a format, issuer path or revocation behaviour, so they remain two candidate families. A HubSpot statement relating them would settle it.

HubSpot's changelog says creation of new legacy private apps is being disabled from 2026-09-28 (new accounts) and 2026-10-26 (older accounts) while existing ones keep working. Any contract for this family is therefore bounded to tokens already issued; whether tokens of new Service Keys or project-based static auth tokens share this shape is not established.
